title: Equity and Trusts
topics: Resulting and constructive trusts (incl. the family home)
Breach of trust, tracing and third-party liability

notes.h: The nature of equity and the trust
notes.body:
Equity is the body of rules first developed by the Court of Chancery to soften the rigidity of the common law. In the Earl of Oxford's Case (1615) it was settled that where equity and common law conflict, equity prevails. The Judicature Acts 1873–75 merged the courts but not the rules themselves. The rule that equity prevails is now in the Senior Courts Act 1981 s49.

Characteristics.
- Equitable remedies are discretionary. They include specific performance, injunctions (interim injunctions under American Cyanamid v Ethicon [1975]), rescission, rectification and account.
- Equity acts in personam, against the defendant's conscience (Penn v Lord Baltimore (1750)).
- The maxims guide the discretion rather than binding it: those who come to equity must have clean hands, delay defeats equity, equity regards as done what ought to be done, and equity will not assist a volunteer.
- The fusion debate asks whether law and equity are now one system. Lord Diplock thought so in United Scientific Holdings v Burnley BC [1978]. Most commentators accept only procedural fusion, while recognising that doctrines borrow from each other, as with equitable compensation.

The trust. A trust arises where a trustee holds property for beneficiaries or for a permitted purpose. Legal title sits with the trustee, and the beneficiaries have equitable proprietary rights. Those rights survive the trustee's insolvency and bind anyone except a bona fide purchaser of the legal estate without notice. Trusts are classified as:
- express, arising from the settlor's intention;
- resulting, under the two categories in Re Vandervell's Trusts (No 2) [1974]; and
- constructive, imposed by law. Westdeutsche Landesbank v Islington LBC [1996] confirms that a trust depends on the trustee's conscience being affected and that it needs identifiable trust property.

Trusts compared with other concepts.
- Contract: a trust needs no consideration, and a beneficiary can enforce it without privity.
- Debt: a debtor may mix the money with its own, whereas a trustee must keep trust property separate. Barclays Bank v Quistclose [1970] and Twinsectra v Yardley [2002] show that a loan for a stated purpose can create a trust.
- Powers: a power is discretionary, but a trustee must perform a trust.

Saunders v Vautier (1841): adult beneficiaries of sound mind who together hold the entire beneficial interest can end the trust and call for the property.

Illustration. A customer prepays a mail-order company, which places the money in a separate "customer trust account" (Re Kayford [1975]). The customers are beneficiaries, so if the company fails the money does not go to its creditors.

Exam pitfalls.
- Describe the maxims as guiding principles, not rigid rules.
- Distinguish the trust from contract, debt and agency precisely, using the property-based features.

An express trust needs certainty of intention, subject matter and objects (Knight v Knight (1840)).

Intention. The question is whether the settlor intended to impose a binding obligation. Precatory words such as "in full confidence" usually create only a moral obligation (Re Adams and the Kensington Vestry (1884)), although the whole document must be read (Comiskey v Bowring-Hanbury [1905]). Conduct can be enough: "this money is as much yours as mine" (Paul v Constance [1977]), and a company's separate customer account (Re Kayford [1975]). Sham declarations and lack of segregation tend to defeat a trust (Re Farepak Food and Gifts [2006]).

Subject matter. The trust property must be identifiable. "The bulk of my estate" is too vague (Palmer v Simmonds (1854)). Re Golay's WT [1965] upheld "a reasonable income" as an objective standard. For tangible goods, the specific items must be separated out (Re London Wine [1986]; Re Goldcorp [1995]). For intangibles such as shares of one class, Hunter v Moss [1994] allowed a trust of 50 out of 950 shares without segregation. The beneficial shares must also be certain (Boyce v Boyce (1849)).

Objects.
- Fixed trusts require a complete list of the beneficiaries (IRC v Broadway Cottages [1955]).
- Discretionary trusts and powers use the "is or is not" test: can it be said of any given person whether they are or are not within the class? (McPhail v Doulton [1971]; Re Gulbenkian [1970]). Re Baden's Deed Trusts (No 2) [1973] showed the judges differing on evidential certainty. Re Barlow's WT [1979] treated a gift to "friends" as a series of individual gifts, needing only that particular claimants qualify.
- A trust can also fail for administrative unworkability (R v District Auditor, ex p West Yorkshire MCC [1986]) or for capriciousness.

Formalities (LPA 1925 s53).
- s53(1)(b): a declaration of trust of land must be evidenced in writing.
- s53(1)(c): disposing of a subsisting equitable interest requires signed writing (Grey v IRC [1960]). It does not apply where the legal and equitable titles move together (Vandervell v IRC [1967]).
- s53(2): resulting, implied and constructive trusts are exempt (Neville v Wilson [1997]; compare Oughtred v IRC [1960]).
- Equity will not allow a statute to be used as an instrument of fraud (Rochefoucauld v Boustead [1897]).
- Testamentary trusts must comply with the Wills Act 1837 s9. Fully secret trusts require communication and acceptance during the testator's lifetime (Ottaway v Norman [1972]). Half-secret trusts require communication before or at the time the will is made (Blackwell v Blackwell [1929]; Re Keen [1937]).

Exam pitfalls.
- Do not confuse conceptual certainty with evidential certainty.
- Check which formality section applies before discussing it.

A trust or gift is constituted when the property is vested in the trustee or donee, or the settlor declares themselves trustee. Equity will not perfect an imperfect gift for a volunteer (Milroy v Lord (1862)). A failed gift will not be saved by treating it as a declaration of trust (Richards v Delbridge (1874)).

Methods of transfer.
- Land: deed and registration. Shares: transfer form and registration. Chattels: delivery or deed. Equitable interests: signed writing (LPA s53(1)(c)).

Exceptions where equity intervenes.
- The Re Rose principle: a gift is complete in equity once the donor has done everything within their own power. In Re Rose [1952] the gift took effect once executed transfers were handed over, before registration (also Mascall v Mascall (1984)).
- Unconscionability: Pennington v Waine [2002] held that it would be unconscionable for the donor to recall the gift, even though the share transfer form was never delivered. The decision is widely criticised (contrast Zeital v Kaye [2010] and Curtis v Pulbrook [2011]).
- Choithram v Pagarani [2001]: where a settlor declares a trust and is one of several trustees, the property is bound once it is vested in any one of them.
- Strong v Bird (1874): if the donor appoints the donee as executor, the imperfect gift is perfected, provided the donor's intention continued until death (Re Gonin [1979]).
- Donatio mortis causa: a gift made in contemplation of impending death, conditional on death, with dominion over the property handed over (Sen v Headley [1991]). King v Dubrey [2015] restricted the doctrine and expressed doubts about Vallee v Birchwood [2013].
- Proprietary estoppel can also perfect an incomplete gift of land.

Covenants to settle.
- A volunteer cannot enforce a covenant to settle property: equity will not help (Re Plumptre's Marriage Settlement [1910]). Nor will the court direct trustees to sue on it (Re Pryce [1917]; Re Kay's Settlement [1939]).
- Spouses and issue (within the marriage consideration) can enforce it.
- A trust of the benefit of the covenant can be enforced (Fletcher v Fletcher (1844)).
- Cannon v Hartley [1949]: a party to a deed may recover damages at common law.
- The Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 may give an identified beneficiary a right to sue.
- Re Ralli's WT [1964]: once property comes into the trustee's hands by any route, the trust is constituted.

Illustration. Mo hands his niece a signed share transfer and certificate, then dies before registration. Under Re Rose the gift is complete in equity.

Exam pitfalls.
- Identify the type of property and the required method of transfer first.
- Do not apply Pennington without first noting the criticism of it.

notes.h: Charitable trusts and non-charitable purpose trusts
notes.body:
Charities enjoy tax relief and are exempt from the beneficiary principle, the rule against perpetual duration and certainty of objects. The Charity Commission regulates them.

Definition (Charities Act 2011). A charitable purpose falls within one of the 13 heads in s3(1) and is for the public benefit (s4). The heads include the prevention or relief of poverty, the advancement of education, religion and health, amateur sport, animal welfare, and a residual head carrying over earlier law (s3(1)(m)). Section 4(2) removes any presumption of public benefit. The purpose must also be exclusively charitable (s1).

Public benefit has two aspects.
- Benefit: an identifiable benefit to the public, assessed on evidence (National Anti-Vivisection Society v IRC [1948]; Gilmour v Coats [1949] on purely private prayer).
- Public: a sufficient section of the public. A personal nexus fails (Oppenheim v Tobacco Securities Trust [1951]; Re Compton [1945]). Poverty trusts are the exception (Dingle v Turner [1972]; AG v Charity Commission [2012] UT). Fee-charging schools must provide more than token benefit for the poor (R (Independent Schools Council) v Charity Commission [2011] UT).

Political purposes. A trust whose main purpose is to change the law or government policy is not charitable (McGovern v AG [1982]). Campaigning that is merely ancillary to charitable purposes is acceptable.

Cy-près (Charities Act 2011 s62). Where a charitable purpose fails, the property can be applied to similar purposes.
- Initial failure requires a general charitable intention (Re Rymer [1895]; contrast Re Harwood [1936]).
- Subsequent failure needs no such intention, because the property has already been dedicated to charity.
- A gift to a charity that has merely changed form is still valid.

Non-charitable purpose trusts. These are generally void under the beneficiary principle (Morice v Bishop of Durham (1805); Re Astor's ST [1952]; Re Endacott [1960]).
- Anomalous valid exceptions: maintaining tombs (Re Hooper [1932]), specific animals (Re Dean (1889)) and the hunting case of Re Thompson [1934]. They must not exceed the common law perpetuity period, which is usually 21 years.
- Re Denley's Trust Deed [1969]: a purpose trust that directly benefits ascertainable individuals is valid.

Gifts to unincorporated associations. These usually take effect as an accretion to the funds, held on contract-holding terms under the club's rules (Neville Estates v Madden [1962]; Re Recher's WT [1972]; Re Lipinski's WT [1976]). On dissolution, the surplus is usually shared among the members at that time (Re Bucks Constabulary Fund (No 2) [1979]).

Exam pitfalls.
- Charitable status requires both a head and public benefit. The exclusivity requirement can defeat it, as with "charitable or benevolent" (Chichester Diocesan Fund v Simpson [1944]).
- Keep initial failure and subsequent failure separate.

notes.h: Resulting and constructive trusts, including the family home
notes.body:
Resulting trusts. Megarry J in Re Vandervell's Trusts (No 2) [1974] identified two kinds.
- Presumed resulting trusts arise on a voluntary transfer to another, or where one person pays the purchase price for property put in another's name (Dyer v Dyer (1788)). The presumption is rebuttable by evidence of a gift. The presumption of advancement still applies between father and child and from husband to wife, because the Equality Act 2010 s199, which abolishes it, is not in force. In modern conditions it is weak (Pettitt v Pettitt [1970]). Under Patel v Mirza [2016], illegality is decided on a policy-based "range of factors" approach, replacing Tinsley v Milligan [1994].
- Automatic resulting trusts arise where an express trust fails or does not dispose of the whole beneficial interest (Vandervell v IRC [1967]; Re Gillingham Bus Disaster Fund [1958]). Westdeutsche [1996] explained both as giving effect to presumed intention, a view that is debated.

Common intention constructive trusts of the family home.
- Sole name. The claimant must show an express agreement, arrangement or understanding to share, together with detrimental reliance (Lloyds Bank v Rosset [1991]; Eves v Eves [1975]; Grant v Edwards [1986]). Rosset's dictum that direct contributions alone would support an inference has been doubted since Stack v Dowden [2007] and Abbott v Abbott [2007].
- Joint names. Equity follows the law: the starting point is beneficial joint tenancy (Stack v Dowden [2007]). The claimant must show a different common intention, inferred from the whole course of dealing. Stack lists factors such as discussions, purpose and finances.
- Quantification. Under Jones v Kernott [2011], intention is first inferred from conduct. Where no common intention as to shares can be found, the court may impute one and award what it considers fair, having regard to the whole course of dealing.
- Investment property: contrast Laskar v Laskar [2008] (resulting trust) with Marr v Collie [2017] PC.

Other constructive trusts.
- Bribes and secret commissions received by a fiduciary are held on constructive trust (FHR European Ventures v Cedar Capital [2014]).
- Specifically enforceable contracts of sale (Lysaght v Edwards (1876)).
- Pallant v Morgan [1953] joint-venture equities (Banner Homes v Luff [2000]; contrast Crossco No 4 v Jolan [2011]).
- Mutual wills (Re Goodchild [1997]).
- Unconscionable reliance on the absence of formality (Rochefoucauld v Boustead [1897]).

Illustration. Kay, the sole owner, tells Lou "this is our home", and Lou pays half the deposit. Lou has a Rosset agreement plus reliance.

Exam pitfalls.
- Decide first whether the property is in a sole name or joint names.
- Do not impute an intention to share at the acquisition stage in a sole-name case.

Trustees must learn the trust terms, get in the property, and act unanimously, personally and in the beneficiaries' interests.

The duty of care. Trustee Act 2000 s1 requires the care and skill that is reasonable in the circumstances. The standard is higher for a trustee with special knowledge or acting in a professional capacity. The duty applies to investment, delegation and the other functions listed in Sch 1. The earlier standard was the ordinary prudent business person (Speight v Gaunt (1883)).

Investment.
- s3: the general power of investment, allowing trustees to invest as if absolutely entitled. Land can be acquired under s8.
- s4: trustees must consider the standard investment criteria, meaning suitability and diversification, and review the investments.
- s5: proper advice, unless unnecessary or inappropriate.
- Their primary aim is the beneficiaries' financial interest (Cowan v Scargill [1985]). Ethical exclusions are acceptable where they are consistent with that aim, or for charities where an investment conflicts with the charity's purposes (Butler-Sloss v Charity Commission [2022]).
- Bartlett v Barclays Bank Trust Co [1980] required a professional trustee to monitor a company in which the trust held a controlling stake. Nestle v NatWest Bank [1993] showed that a claimant must prove loss caused by the failure.

Delegation. Trustees may delegate administrative functions to agents (TA 2000 s11), but not distributive discretions. For asset management they need a policy statement (s15), and they must review the arrangements (s22).

Maintenance and advancement.
- TA 1925 s31 allows income to be applied for the maintenance, education or benefit of a minor beneficiary.
- s32 allows capital to be advanced for a beneficiary's benefit. For trusts created or arising after 1 October 2014 this can be up to the whole of the beneficiary's presumptive share (Inheritance and Trustees' Powers Act 2014 s9). Before that the limit was one-half. "Benefit" is construed widely (Pilkington v IRC [1964]).

Discretions and disclosure. Trustees must consider exercising their discretions, take relevant matters into account, and act within their powers and for proper purposes. Pitt v Holt [2013] narrowed the Hastings-Bass rule: a decision is voidable only if the trustees breached their duty by failing to consider relevant matters. Beneficiaries have no automatic right to see the reasons for trustees' decisions (Re Londonderry's Settlement [1965]). Disclosure of trust documents is in the court's supervisory discretion (Schmidt v Rosewood Trust [2003]).

Appointment and remuneration. Trustees are appointed under TA 1925 s36, by the court (s41), or at beneficiaries' direction (TOLATA s19). Professionals may be paid (TA 2000 ss28–29).

Exam pitfalls.
- Apply the statutory investment duties in sequence: power, criteria, advice, review.
- Remember that loss and causation must be proved.

A fiduciary is someone who has undertaken to act for or on behalf of another in circumstances giving rise to a relationship of trust and confidence. The defining obligation is loyalty (Bristol & West BS v Mothew [1998]). Settled categories include trustees, directors, agents, solicitors and partners; others can arise on the facts.

Core duties. These are proscriptive: they tell the fiduciary what not to do.
- No-conflict: the fiduciary must not put themselves in a position where duty and interest conflict, or may conflict.
- No-profit: the fiduciary must not profit from their position without fully informed consent (Bray v Ford [1896]).
- Self-dealing: a trustee's purchase of trust property can be set aside by any beneficiary, however fair the price (Tito v Waddell (No 2) [1977]; but see Holder v Holder [1968]).
- Fair-dealing: buying a beneficiary's interest stands only if fair and fully disclosed.

The strictness of the rule.
- Keech v Sandford (1726): a trustee who took a lease renewal for himself, which the landlord refused to the trust, held it on trust.
- Regal (Hastings) v Gulliver [1942]: directors were liable for profits from an opportunity that came to them as directors, despite good faith and the company's inability to take it.
- Boardman v Phipps [1967]: a solicitor and a beneficiary who used information obtained while acting for the trust held their profits on constructive trust, although they had benefited the trust. They received an allowance for their work, but allowances are restricted (Guinness v Saunders [1990]).
- Rukhadze v Recovery Partners GP Ltd [2025] UKSC 10: the Supreme Court refused to relax the strict profit rule or to introduce a "but for" causation test.

Remedies.
- An account of profits, or equitable compensation for loss.
- A bribe or secret commission is held on constructive trust (FHR European Ventures v Cedar Capital [2014], overruling Lister v Stubbs (1890) and disapproving Sinclair v Versailles [2011]). A proprietary remedy gives priority on insolvency and the right to trace and to claim any increase in value (AG for Hong Kong v Reid [1994]).
- Fully informed consent or the trust instrument can authorise what would otherwise be a breach.
- For directors, the duties are codified in Companies Act 2006 ss175–177 (see Bhullar v Bhullar [2003]).

Illustration. A trustee who learns of a cheap site through the trust and buys it holds it on trust, even if the trust could not afford it.

Exam pitfalls.
- Not every duty a fiduciary owes is a fiduciary duty. Breach of the duty of care is not a breach of loyalty (Mothew).
- Honesty and benefit to the principal are not defences. Only fully informed consent is.

notes.h: Breach of trust, tracing and third-party liability
notes.body:
Personal liability of trustees. A trustee in breach must restore the loss to the trust fund. AIB Group v Mark Redler [2014] confirmed Target Holdings v Redferns [1996]: compensation is assessed with hindsight at trial and requires causation. Liability is joint and several, with contribution under the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978. Passivity is no ground for indemnity (Bahin v Hughes (1886)); indemnity is exceptional, as where a solicitor-trustee controlled matters (Head v Gould [1898]).

Defences.
- TA 1925 s61: relief for a trustee who acted honestly and reasonably and ought fairly to be excused.
- Consent or instigation by a beneficiary (Re Pauling's ST [1964]). Section 62 allows the court to impound that beneficiary's interest.
- Exemption clauses can exclude liability for negligence, even gross negligence, but not for dishonesty (Armitage v Nurse [1998]).
- Limitation: six years under the Limitation Act 1980 s21(3). There is no period for fraud, or for recovering trust property from the trustee (s21(1)). Section 21(1) does not cover strangers such as dishonest assistants (Williams v Central Bank of Nigeria [2014]).

Tracing identifies a substitute for the claimant's property; it is a process, not a claim (Foskett v McKeown [2001]).
- Unmixed substitute: claim the asset or a lien over it.
- Trustee mixing with own money: the trustee is presumed to spend their own money first (Re Hallett (1880)), but the beneficiary may claim investments made from the mixed account (Re Oatway [1903]). The claim is capped at the lowest intermediate balance (Roscoe v Winder [1915]).
- Two innocent beneficiaries' funds mixed: Clayton's Case (first in, first out) is usually displaced in favour of shares in proportion to contributions (Barlow Clowes v Vaughan [1992]; Russell-Cooke v Prentis [2002]).
- An innocent volunteer who mixes shares rateably (Re Diplock [1948]).
- Backwards tracing needs coordination between depletion and acquisition (Federal Republic of Brazil v Durant [2015] PC).
- Tracing ends against a bona fide purchaser or on dissipation.

Third-party liability.
- Dishonest assistance requires a breach of trust or fiduciary duty, assistance in it, and dishonesty (Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan [1995]). Dishonesty is objective, judged by ordinary standards against the defendant's actual knowledge (Ivey v Genting [2017]; Group Seven v Notable Services [2019]).
- Knowing receipt requires a disposal of assets in breach of trust, beneficial receipt of property traceable to that breach, and knowledge that makes it unconscionable to retain the benefit (BCCI v Akindele [2001]). The claimant must still have had an equitable interest at the time of receipt (Byers v Saudi National Bank [2023]).

Exam pitfalls.
- Keep personal claims (compensation, assistance, receipt) separate from proprietary claims (tracing).
- Apply the correct tracing rule to each pattern of mixing.

cards.f: What did the Earl of Oxford's Case (1615) establish?
cards.b: Where common law and equity conflict, equity prevails. The rule is now in the Senior Courts Act 1981 s49.

cards.f: What did the Judicature Acts 1873–75 do?
cards.b: They merged the common law courts and the Court of Chancery into one Supreme Court, which administers both systems. Most commentators say the rules themselves were not merged.

cards.f: What does it mean that equity acts in personam?
cards.b: Equitable orders are directed at the defendant personally and their conscience, so English courts can make orders about property abroad (Penn v Lord Baltimore (1750)).

cards.f: State the rule in Saunders v Vautier (1841).
cards.b: Adult beneficiaries of sound mind who are together entitled to the whole beneficial interest can end the trust and call for the legal title, whatever the settlor wished.

cards.f: How does a trust differ from a debt?
cards.b: A debtor may use the money as its own and owes only a personal obligation to repay. A trustee must keep the property separate, and the beneficiaries' proprietary rights survive the trustee's insolvency.

cards.f: What is a Quistclose trust?
cards.b: Money lent for a specific purpose and not to be used freely by the borrower is held on trust. If the purpose fails, the money is held for the lender (Barclays Bank v Quistclose [1970]; Twinsectra v Yardley [2002]).

cards.f: What is the difference between a trust and a power?
cards.b: A trust is mandatory: the trustee must carry it out. A power is discretionary, so the holder must consider whether to exercise it but need not do so.

cards.f: What principles did Lord Browne-Wilkinson set out in Westdeutsche v Islington [1996]?
cards.b: Equity acts on the conscience of the legal owner, a trust needs identifiable property, and the beneficiary's interest is proprietary and binds everyone except a bona fide purchaser without notice.

cards.f: What is the fusion debate?
cards.b: Whether law and equity have merged into one system since 1875. Lord Diplock said yes in United Scientific Holdings [1978]. The mainstream view accepts administrative fusion while doctrines continue to influence each other.

cards.f: Name four equitable maxims.
cards.b: Those who come to equity must come with clean hands; delay defeats equity; equity regards as done what ought to be done; equity will not assist a volunteer.

cards.f: What are the three certainties?
cards.b: Certainty of intention, of subject matter and of objects (Knight v Knight (1840)).

cards.f: Why was there a trust in Paul v Constance [1977]?
cards.b: Mr Constance repeatedly told his partner the bank money was "as much yours as mine". Read in context, that showed an intention to hold it on trust for both of them.

cards.f: What did Hunter v Moss [1994] decide?
cards.b: A trust of 50 of a settlor's 950 shares in one company was valid without segregation, because the shares were identical intangibles. Contrast Re London Wine [1986] for tangible goods.

cards.f: What test of certainty of objects applies to discretionary trusts?
cards.b: The "is or is not" test: whether it can be said of any given individual that they are or are not a member of the class (McPhail v Doulton [1971]).

cards.f: What test applies to a fixed trust?
cards.b: The complete list test: it must be possible to draw up a full list of every beneficiary (IRC v Broadway Cottages [1955]).

cards.f: What is administrative unworkability?
cards.b: A discretionary trust whose class is so wide that it cannot be administered sensibly is void, even if the class is conceptually certain (R v District Auditor, ex p West Yorkshire MCC [1986]).

cards.f: What does LPA 1925 s53(1)(c) require, and what did Grey v IRC [1960] decide?
cards.b: A disposition of a subsisting equitable interest must be in signed writing. Grey held that an oral direction to trustees to hold for others was such a disposition and was ineffective.

cards.f: Why did s53(1)(c) not apply in Vandervell v IRC [1967]?
cards.b: The beneficial owner told his bare trustee to transfer the legal title to a third party. When legal and equitable title pass together, separate writing is not needed.

cards.f: What are the requirements of a fully secret trust?
cards.b: The testator intended to create a trust, communicated it to the legatee during the testator's lifetime, and the legatee accepted, expressly or by silence (Ottaway v Norman [1972]).

cards.f: When must a half-secret trust be communicated?
cards.b: Before or at the same time as the will is executed, consistently with the will's terms (Blackwell v Blackwell [1929]; Re Keen [1937]).

cards.f: What three methods of making a gift or trust were identified in Milroy v Lord (1862)?
cards.b: An outright transfer to the donee, a transfer to trustees on trust, or a declaration of oneself as trustee. A failed method will not be rescued by treating it as another.

cards.f: What is the Re Rose [1952] principle?
cards.b: A gift is complete in equity once the donor has done everything within their own power to transfer the property, even if a third party, such as the company registrar, still has to act.

cards.f: Why is Pennington v Waine [2002] controversial?
cards.b: The gift of shares was held complete although the transfer form was never delivered, on the ground that recall would be unconscionable. That arguably undermines the rule that equity will not assist a volunteer.

cards.f: What did Choithram v Pagarani [2001] decide?
cards.b: Where a settlor declares that property is held on a trust of which he is one of several trustees, the trust is constituted once the property is in his hands, even without transfer to the other trustees.

cards.f: What is the rule in Strong v Bird (1874)?
cards.b: An imperfect lifetime gift is perfected when the donee becomes the donor's executor, provided the donor's intention to give continued until death.

cards.f: What are the requirements of a donatio mortis causa?
cards.b: The gift must be made in contemplation of impending death, conditional on that death, and with dominion over the property, or the means of controlling it, handed over (King v Dubrey [2015]; Sen v Headley [1991]).

cards.f: Can a volunteer enforce a covenant to settle?
cards.b: No. Equity will not assist, and the court will direct trustees not to sue on the volunteer's behalf (Re Pryce [1917]; Re Kay's Settlement [1939]). Those within the marriage consideration can enforce it.

cards.f: What did Fletcher v Fletcher (1844) decide?
cards.b: A covenant to pay money to trustees created a completely constituted trust of the benefit of the promise, which the volunteer beneficiary could enforce.

cards.f: What is the significance of Re Ralli's WT [1964]?
cards.b: If the intended trust property reaches the trustee by any route, here as executor, the trust is constituted and the beneficiaries can enforce it.

cards.f: How can the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 help a volunteer?
cards.b: If the covenant to settle expressly confers a benefit on the beneficiary, or purports to, and that person is identified, they may enforce it directly as a third party.

cards.f: What two requirements must a charitable purpose meet under the Charities Act 2011?
cards.b: It must fall within one of the s3(1) heads and be for the public benefit (s4). The institution's purposes must also be exclusively charitable.

cards.f: What is the personal nexus test?
cards.b: Beneficiaries defined by a relationship with a named person or employer are not a section of the public (Oppenheim v Tobacco Securities Trust [1951]). Poverty trusts are the exception (Dingle v Turner [1972]).

cards.f: Why was the trust in Gilmour v Coats [1949] not charitable?
cards.b: Intercessory prayer by an enclosed order of nuns gave no benefit to the public that could be proved, and edification by example was too vague.

cards.f: When is a political purpose fatal to charitable status?
cards.b: When the main purpose is to change the law or government policy, at home or abroad (McGovern v AG [1982]). Ancillary campaigning in furtherance of charitable purposes is allowed.

cards.f: When must there be a general charitable intention for cy-près?
cards.b: Only on initial failure, where the purpose is impossible when the gift takes effect (Re Rymer [1895]). It is not needed for subsequent failure.

cards.f: What is the beneficiary principle?
cards.b: A private trust must have ascertainable beneficiaries who can enforce it, so non-charitable purpose trusts are generally void (Morice v Bishop of Durham (1805); Re Astor [1952]).

cards.f: What are the anomalous exceptions to the beneficiary principle?
cards.b: Trusts for the maintenance of particular tombs and monuments, for particular animals, and a few others such as saying private masses. They must be limited to the perpetuity period (Re Endacott [1960]).

cards.f: What did Re Denley's Trust Deed [1969] decide?
cards.b: A trust of land for a sports ground, mainly for a company's employees, was valid because it directly benefited ascertainable individuals with standing to enforce it.

cards.f: How are gifts to unincorporated associations usually analysed?
cards.b: As gifts to the current members, to be held as an accretion to the funds under their contract with each other through the rules (Re Recher's WT [1972]; Neville Estates v Madden [1962]).

cards.f: Why did the gift in Chichester Diocesan Fund v Simpson [1944] fail?
cards.b: Charitable "or benevolent" objects were not exclusively charitable, because benevolent purposes could include non-charitable ones.

cards.f: What are the two categories of resulting trust in Re Vandervell's Trusts (No 2) [1974]?
cards.b: Presumed resulting trusts, arising from a voluntary transfer or a purchase in another's name, and automatic resulting trusts, arising where the beneficial interest is not fully disposed of.

cards.f: What is the presumption of advancement, and what is its current status?
cards.b: A presumption of gift for transfers from father to child or husband to wife. The Equality Act 2010 s199 would abolish it but is not in force, and the presumption is now weak.

cards.f: What did Lloyds Bank v Rosset [1991] require for a sole-name constructive trust?
cards.b: Evidence of an express agreement, arrangement or understanding to share beneficially, plus detrimental reliance. Otherwise direct contributions to the price from which a common intention could be inferred.

cards.f: What is the starting point for a home in joint names, according to Stack v Dowden [2007]?
cards.b: Equity follows the law, so the parties are presumed beneficial joint tenants. A party claiming otherwise must prove a different common intention.

cards.f: What did Jones v Kernott [2011] add?
cards.b: The common intention can change over time. Where it is clear the parties intended different shares but their intention about the size of those shares cannot be found, the court may impute a fair share having regard to the whole course of dealing.

cards.f: How did Patel v Mirza [2016] change the illegality defence?
cards.b: It replaced the reliance test in Tinsley v Milligan with a policy-based approach. The court considers the purpose of the prohibition, other relevant public policies and proportionality.

cards.f: What did FHR European Ventures v Cedar Capital [2014] decide?
cards.b: A bribe or secret commission received by an agent in breach of fiduciary duty is held on constructive trust for the principal.

cards.f: What is a Pallant v Morgan equity?
cards.b: Where parties agree that one will acquire property for their joint benefit and the other refrains from competing, the acquirer holds on constructive trust (Banner Homes v Luff [2000]).

cards.f: What is an automatic resulting trust? Give an example.
cards.b: One arising by operation of law where a trust fails or leaves surplus. In Re Gillingham Bus Disaster Fund [1958], surplus donations went back to the donors on resulting trust.

cards.f: What did Laskar v Laskar [2008] decide?
cards.b: Where a property bought in joint names was mainly an investment, a resulting trust analysis based on contributions was more appropriate than the Stack v Dowden presumption.

cards.f: What is the statutory duty of care for trustees?
cards.b: Trustee Act 2000 s1: such care and skill as is reasonable in the circumstances, with a higher standard for trustees with special knowledge or acting professionally.

cards.f: What are the standard investment criteria?
cards.b: Under TA 2000 s4: the suitability of the investment to the trust and the need for diversification so far as appropriate. Trustees must also review investments from time to time.

cards.f: What did Cowan v Scargill [1985] decide?
cards.b: Trustees of a pension fund must put the beneficiaries' financial interests first and could not reject profitable investments because of personal or political views.

cards.f: Why is Butler-Sloss v Charity Commission [2022] significant?
cards.b: It held that charity trustees may exclude investments that conflict with the charity's purposes, after weighing the financial effect, so climate-aligned investment policies can be lawful.

cards.f: Which functions can trustees not delegate under TA 2000 s11?
cards.b: Distributive functions (deciding who gets what), the power to appoint trustees, and decisions about whether to allocate payments to capital or income.

cards.f: What does TA 1925 s32 allow?
cards.b: Trustees may advance capital for the benefit of a beneficiary with an interest in capital. For trusts created after 1 October 2014 this can be up to the whole presumptive share.

cards.f: What did Pitt v Holt [2013] decide about the Hastings-Bass rule?
cards.b: A trustee's decision is voidable only if failing to consider relevant matters amounted to a breach of duty. An error alone is not enough.

cards.f: What did Re Londonderry's Settlement [1965] decide?
cards.b: Beneficiaries are not entitled to see documents revealing trustees' reasons for exercising dispositive discretions.

cards.f: What did Bartlett v Barclays Bank Trust Co [1980] decide?
cards.b: A professional trustee holding a controlling stake had to monitor the company's affairs, and was liable for losses from failing to do so.

cards.f: Under which provisions may beneficiaries direct trustee appointments?
cards.b: TOLATA 1996 s19: adult beneficiaries of full capacity who together are absolutely entitled may direct trustees to retire or appoint new trustees, unless the trust instrument excludes this.

cards.f: How did Millett LJ define a fiduciary in Bristol & West v Mothew [1998]?
cards.b: Someone who has undertaken to act for or on behalf of another in circumstances giving rise to a relationship of trust and confidence. The distinguishing obligation is loyalty.

cards.f: What did Keech v Sandford (1726) decide?
cards.b: A trustee who took a renewal of a lease for himself, after the landlord refused to renew for the infant beneficiary, held it on trust for the beneficiary.

cards.f: Why were the directors liable in Regal (Hastings) v Gulliver [1942]?
cards.b: They made a profit from shares they acquired because of their position as directors. Their good faith and the company's inability to buy were irrelevant.

cards.f: What did Boardman v Phipps [1967] decide?
cards.b: Fiduciaries who used information obtained while acting for a trust to make a profit had to account for it, though they acted honestly and the trust also gained. They received an allowance for their skill and work.

cards.f: What is the self-dealing rule?
cards.b: A trustee's purchase of trust property is voidable at the instance of any beneficiary, however fair the price, unless authorised or approved by the court (Tito v Waddell (No 2) [1977]).

cards.f: How does the fair-dealing rule differ from the self-dealing rule?
cards.b: When a trustee buys a beneficiary's own beneficial interest, the deal stands if the trustee took no advantage and made full disclosure, and the transaction was fair.

cards.f: What did Industrial Development Consultants v Cooley [1972] decide?
cards.b: A managing director who secured a contract for himself that he learned of while acting for the company had to account for the profits.

cards.f: What did Rukhadze v Recovery Partners GP Ltd [2025] UKSC 10 decide?
cards.b: The Supreme Court refused to soften the strict profit rule, declining to adopt a test asking whether the fiduciary would have made the profit anyway.

cards.f: What defence is available to a fiduciary who has profited?
cards.b: Fully informed consent of the principal, or authorisation in the trust instrument. Good faith and benefit to the principal are not defences.

cards.f: Which sections codify directors' conflict duties?
cards.b: Companies Act 2006 s175 (avoid conflicts), s176 (no benefits from third parties) and s177 (declare interests in proposed transactions).

cards.f: What did AIB Group v Mark Redler [2014] decide?
cards.b: Equitable compensation for breach of trust is assessed with hindsight at trial and is limited to loss caused by the breach, applying Target Holdings v Redferns [1996].

cards.f: What is the effect of TA 1925 s61?
cards.b: The court may relieve a trustee from liability, wholly or partly, if they acted honestly and reasonably and ought fairly to be excused.

cards.f: What limit on exemption clauses did Armitage v Nurse [1998] set?
cards.b: A trustee exemption clause can exclude liability for negligence, even gross negligence, but not for dishonesty or fraud, because the core trust obligation of honesty is irreducible.

cards.f: What are the limitation periods for breach of trust?
cards.b: Six years under the Limitation Act 1980 s21(3). There is no period for fraudulent breach or for recovering trust property from the trustee (s21(1)).

cards.f: What is the rule in Re Hallett's Estate (1880)?
cards.b: A trustee who mixes trust money with their own in an account is presumed to spend their own money first.

cards.f: What is the lowest intermediate balance rule?
cards.b: A beneficiary cannot trace into a mixed account for more than the lowest balance it reached between the trust money being paid in and the claim (Roscoe v Winder [1915]).

cards.f: How do courts trace where two innocent beneficiaries' funds are mixed?
cards.b: Clayton's Case (first in, first out) is usually displaced as unfair and impractical, in favour of shares in proportion to contributions (Barlow Clowes v Vaughan [1992]; Russell-Cooke v Prentis [2002]).

cards.f: What are the elements of dishonest assistance?
cards.b: A breach of trust or fiduciary duty, assistance by the defendant, and dishonesty, judged objectively against the defendant's actual knowledge (Royal Brunei v Tan [1995]; Ivey v Genting [2017]).

cards.f: What test of knowledge applies to knowing receipt?
cards.b: Whether the recipient's state of knowledge makes it unconscionable to keep the benefit of the receipt (BCCI v Akindele [2001]).

cards.f: What did Byers v Saudi National Bank [2023] decide?
cards.b: Knowing receipt requires the claimant to have a continuing equitable proprietary interest in the asset when the defendant receives it. If that interest has been extinguished, there is no claim.

cards.f: What did Foskett v McKeown [2001] decide?
cards.b: Beneficiaries whose money paid some of the premiums on a life policy could trace into the payout and take a proportionate share of it. Tracing vindicates property rights, not unjust enrichment.

questions.q: Under the rule in Saunders v Vautier (1841), who may bring a trust to an end?
options: The trustees acting unanimously
The settlor at any time
Adult beneficiaries of sound mind who together are absolutely entitled
Any single beneficiary with a vested interest
questions.why: Beneficiaries who are all adult, of sound mind and together entitled to the whole beneficial interest may end the trust and call for the property.

questions.q: Which provision requires a declaration of trust of land to be evidenced in writing?
options: Wills Act 1837 s9
questions.why: Section 53(1)(b) requires a declaration of trust respecting land to be manifested and proved by signed writing. Section 53(1)(c) concerns dispositions of existing equitable interests.

questions.q: A settlor leaves £1m to trustees to distribute "among such of my former employees and their relatives as the trustees think fit". Which test of certainty of objects applies?
options: The complete list test from IRC v Broadway Cottages
The "is or is not" test from McPhail v Doulton
The one-person test from Re Barlow
No test, because trustees have a discretion
questions.why: This is a discretionary trust, so McPhail v Doulton [1971] applies: can it be said of any given person whether they are or are not within the class?

questions.q: A donor signs a share transfer form and hands it, with the share certificate, to the donee, but dies before the company registers the transfer. What is the most likely result?
options: The gift fails because legal title never passed
The gift is complete in equity under Re Rose
The shares pass under the donor's will
The gift is valid only if the donee was the donor's executor
questions.why: Under Re Rose [1952] the donor had done everything within his power, so the donor held the shares on trust for the donee until registration.

questions.q: A trust to provide scholarships for the children of employees of Big Plc (which has 100,000 employees) is most likely to be:
options: Charitable, as the advancement of education for a large class
Not charitable, because of the personal nexus to the employer
Charitable, as relief of poverty
Void for uncertainty of objects
questions.why: Oppenheim v Tobacco Securities Trust [1951]: a class defined by employment with a particular company is not a section of the public, however large it is.

questions.q: Ann and Ben buy a house in joint names with no declaration of trust. Ann paid 70% of the price. Following Stack v Dowden, what is the starting point?
options: Ann 70%, Ben 30% on a resulting trust
Beneficial joint tenancy, unless a different common intention is shown
Ann holds the whole on a presumed resulting trust
The court imputes whatever shares it considers fair
questions.why: In a domestic joint-names case, equity follows the law and presumes a beneficial joint tenancy. Unequal contributions alone will not usually displace it.

questions.q: Which statute sets out the general statutory duty of care of trustees?
options: Trustee Act 1925 s61
Trustee Act 2000 s1
Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996 s19
Charities Act 2011 s4
questions.why: TA 2000 s1 requires care and skill reasonable in the circumstances. Section 61 of the 1925 Act is a relieving provision.

questions.q: Directors of Regal bought shares in a subsidiary in good faith when Regal itself could not afford them, and later sold at a profit. According to Regal (Hastings) v Gulliver [1942], the directors:
options: Were not liable because Regal could not have made the profit
Were not liable because they acted in good faith
Were liable to account for the profit because it arose from their fiduciary position
Were liable only for Regal's actual losses
questions.why: The no-profit rule is strict. Good faith and the company's inability to take the opportunity are irrelevant without fully informed consent from the shareholders.

questions.q: Tom, a trustee, pays £10,000 of trust money into his personal account, which already holds £2,000. He withdraws and spends £11,000 on a holiday, then later pays in £5,000 of his own money. The account now holds £6,000. How much can the beneficiaries claim from the account by tracing?
questions.why: The balance fell to £1,000 (£12,000 − £11,000) before later payments in. Under Roscoe v Winder [1915] the claim is capped at that lowest intermediate balance, unless the later deposit was intended to repay the trust.

questions.q: Which statement about donationes mortis causa reflects King v Dubrey [2015]?
options: Any gift made by an elderly person is a valid DMC
The donor must contemplate death in the near future for a specific reason, and the gift must be conditional on death
A DMC cannot apply to land
Dominion can be satisfied by an oral promise alone
questions.why: The Court of Appeal stressed that the doctrine is anomalous and narrow: death must be contemplated in the near future for a specific reason, the gift must be conditional on death, and dominion must be parted with.

questions.q: Name the three certainties required for an express private trust and give one case illustrating each.
markScheme: Intention, e.g. Paul v Constance or Re Adams and Kensington Vestry
Subject matter, e.g. Palmer v Simmonds, Re London Wine or Hunter v Moss
Objects, e.g. McPhail v Doulton or IRC v Broadway Cottages
questions.modelAnswer: Knight v Knight (1840) requires three certainties. Certainty of intention means the settlor must intend to impose a binding trust. Paul v Constance [1977] found such intention in informal words, while Re Adams and the Kensington Vestry (1884) treated precatory words as insufficient. Certainty of subject matter means the property and the beneficial shares must be identifiable. "The bulk" of an estate failed in Palmer v Simmonds (1854). Certainty of objects means the beneficiaries must be ascertainable, under the complete list test for fixed trusts (IRC v Broadway Cottages [1955]) or the "is or is not" test for discretionary trusts (McPhail v Doulton [1971]).

questions.q: Explain how a Quistclose trust shows the difference between a trust and a loan.
markScheme: Normally a loan creates only a personal debt; the money belongs to the borrower
Where money is lent for a specific purpose and is not at the borrower's free disposal, it is held on trust (Barclays v Quistclose)
Twinsectra v Yardley: the lender retains the beneficial interest, subject to the borrower's power to apply the money for the purpose
Consequence: if the purpose fails or the borrower becomes insolvent, the money is returned to the lender rather than going to general creditors
questions.modelAnswer: An ordinary loan creates a debt. The borrower owns the money and owes only a personal obligation to repay, so if the borrower becomes insolvent the lender is an unsecured creditor. In Barclays Bank v Quistclose [1970], however, money lent only to pay a dividend was held on trust when the purpose failed. Lord Millett in Twinsectra v Yardley [2002] explained that the lender keeps the beneficial interest, and the borrower holds the money subject to a power or duty to use it only for the agreed purpose. The money is therefore never at the borrower's free disposal. If the purpose cannot be carried out, it goes back to the lender instead of to the general creditors.

questions.q: Distinguish fully secret and half-secret trusts in terms of the communication requirements, and explain the significance of the difference.
markScheme: Fully secret: the will gives absolutely on its face; communication and acceptance any time before death (Ottaway v Norman; Re Boyes for terms)
Half-secret: the will shows a trust but not its terms; communication before or at execution (Blackwell v Blackwell; Re Keen)
Communication must be consistent with the will in half-secret trusts
The half-secret rule mirrors the probate doctrine of incorporation by reference and is criticised as illogical
Consequence if communication fails: fully secret means the legatee takes beneficially; half-secret means resulting trust for the estate
questions.modelAnswer: A fully secret trust appears on the face of the will as an absolute gift. It binds the legatee if the testator communicated the trust and its terms, and the legatee accepted, at any time before the testator's death (Ottaway v Norman [1972]). Under Re Boyes (1884), terms not communicated mean the legatee holds on resulting trust. A half-secret trust shows a trust on the face of the will. The terms must be communicated before or at the time the will is executed, consistently with the will (Blackwell v Blackwell [1929]; Re Keen [1937]). This rule is criticised as illogical. If communication fails, a fully secret legatee takes beneficially, but a half-secret trustee holds on resulting trust for the estate.

questions.q: Ravi covenanted by deed with trustees to transfer to them, for his nephew, any shares he might inherit from his mother. He has now inherited the shares but refuses to transfer them. Can the nephew or the trustees compel transfer?
markScheme: Future property cannot be held on trust now; the covenant creates only a contractual promise
The nephew is a volunteer outside the marriage consideration; equity will not assist (Re Plumptre)
The trustees will be directed not to sue for damages or specific performance (Re Pryce; Re Kay)

Possible routes: C(RTP)A 1999 if the deed purports to confer a benefit on the nephew; Cannon v Hartley damages only for a party to the deed; Re Ralli if the property reaches the trustees by another route
questions.modelAnswer: The shares were future property when Ravi made the covenant, so no trust could arise then (Re Ellenborough [1903]). The covenant is only a promise by deed. The nephew is a volunteer and is not within the marriage consideration, so equity will not order specific performance (Re Plumptre [1910]). The trustees could sue at common law, but the courts have directed trustees not to sue on behalf of volunteers (Re Pryce [1917]; Re Kay's Settlement [1939]). The nephew may, however, enforce the deed under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 if it purports to benefit him and identifies him. If the shares reach the trustees in some other way, Re Ralli [1964] would treat the trust as constituted.

questions.q: Explain the public benefit requirement for charities after the Charities Act 2006 (now the Charities Act 2011).
markScheme: s4 Charities Act 2011: a purpose must be for the public benefit; no presumption (s4(2))
Benefit aspect: identifiable benefit, balanced against detriment (National Anti-Vivisection Society)
Public aspect: sufficient section of the public; personal nexus fails (Oppenheim)
Poverty exception preserved (Dingle v Turner; AG v Charity Commission [2012])
Fee-charging: more than token benefit to the poor (ISC v Charity Commission [2011])
questions.modelAnswer: Under Charities Act 2011 s4, every charitable purpose must be for the public benefit, and s4(2) removes any presumption that a purpose under a particular head is beneficial. The concept has two aspects. The benefit must be real and identifiable, and the courts weigh it against any harm (National Anti-Vivisection Society v IRC [1948]). The benefit must also reach a sufficient section of the public. A class defined by a personal or employment link fails (Oppenheim [1951]), but poverty trusts are an exception (Dingle v Turner [1972]; AG v Charity Commission [2012]). Fee-charging charities must give the poor more than a token opportunity to benefit (R (Independent Schools Council) v Charity Commission [2011]).

questions.q: How did Jones v Kernott [2011] refine the approach in Stack v Dowden [2007] to quantifying beneficial shares in a jointly owned home?
markScheme: Starting point remains beneficial joint tenancy for joint-names domestic homes
Common intention may be inferred from conduct, and may change over time (ambulatory)
Where it is clear the parties intended different shares but their intention as to quantum cannot be inferred, the court may impute a fair share having regard to the whole course of dealing
Imputation is permitted for quantification, not for establishing the trust in the first place
On the facts, shares of 90/10 reflected the separation and the parties' later financial arrangements
questions.modelAnswer: Jones v Kernott confirmed that, for a home bought in joint names, the starting point is a beneficial joint tenancy. A party who wants a different result must show a different common intention, which can be inferred from the whole course of dealing and can change over time. The Supreme Court then distinguished inference from imputation. Where the parties clearly intended their shares to change but no intention about the size of those shares can be inferred, the court may impute an intention, meaning it awards what is fair in light of the whole course of dealing. On the facts, Mr Kernott took a 10% share, reflecting the long separation during which Ms Jones alone paid for the house.

questions.q: Outline the duties of trustees when making investments under the Trustee Act 2000.
markScheme: General power of investment (s3), as if absolutely entitled
Duty to have regard to standard investment criteria: suitability and diversification (s4(3))
Duty to review investments from time to time (s4(2))
Duty to obtain and consider proper advice unless unnecessary or inappropriate (s5)
questions.modelAnswer: Section 3 gives trustees a general power to invest as if they were absolutely entitled to the trust assets. In exercising it they must have regard to the standard investment criteria in s4: whether investments of that kind, and the particular investment, are suitable for the trust, and the need to diversify so far as is appropriate. They must also review the investments from time to time. Under s5, before investing or reviewing, they must obtain and consider proper advice, unless they reasonably conclude that advice is unnecessary or inappropriate, for example because the sum is small. Throughout, they are subject to the s1 duty of care.

questions.q: Why did the Supreme Court in FHR European Ventures v Cedar Capital [2014] hold that a bribe received by an agent is held on constructive trust, and why does this matter?
markScheme: Rule: benefits obtained by a fiduciary in breach of the no-profit rule are held on trust for the principal
Overruled Lister v Stubbs; approved AG for Hong Kong v Reid; disapproved Sinclair v Versailles
Reasons: consistency (no principled line between bribes and other unauthorised profits), practicality, and policy of deterring breaches
Significance: proprietary claim gives priority on insolvency, tracing into substitutes, and capture of increases in value
Criticism: prejudices unsecured creditors of the fiduciary
questions.modelAnswer: The Court held that any benefit a fiduciary obtains in breach of the no-profit rule belongs in equity to the principal. That covers bribes and secret commissions as well as profits from misused opportunities. Lister v Stubbs (1890) was overruled, AG for Hong Kong v Reid [1994] approved, and Sinclair v Versailles [2011] disapproved on this point. Lord Neuberger relied on consistency, since there is no principled line between bribes and other unauthorised profits, on the simplicity of a single rule, and on the policy of deterring disloyalty. The result matters because a proprietary claim gives the principal priority if the fiduciary is insolvent, allows tracing into substitutes and captures any increase in value. Critics say this harms unsecured creditors.

questions.q: When will a court relieve a trustee from liability under Trustee Act 1925 s61?
markScheme: Trustee acted honestly
Trustee acted reasonably
Trustee ought fairly to be excused for the breach and for omitting to obtain the court's directions
Professional/paid trustees are less readily relieved (eg National Trustees Co of Australasia v General Finance)
questions.modelAnswer: Section 61 lets the court relieve a trustee wholly or partly from personal liability if three conditions are met. The trustee must have acted honestly, and also reasonably, so an honest but careless trustee will not be excused. The court must also consider that the trustee ought fairly to be excused, both for the breach and for not seeking the court's directions. The courts are much slower to relieve paid professional trustees, who are expected to meet higher standards, than unpaid lay trustees who made an understandable mistake. The burden is on the trustee to prove that all three requirements are met.

questions.q: A testator leaves £50,000 "to the Hilltown Chess Club", an unincorporated association, "to be used for the purposes of the club". Analyse the validity of the gift.
markScheme: A gift to an unincorporated association cannot take effect as a gift to the club itself (no legal personality)
Not charitable unless the purposes are charitable (eg advancement of education through chess may qualify; consider public benefit)
Purpose trust analysis would fail the beneficiary principle (Re Astor; Leahy) unless Re Denley applies
Contract-holding analysis: gift to members as an accretion to funds, held under the rules (Re Recher; Re Lipinski)
Valid if members can alter the rules and divide the assets; 'purposes of the club' does not defeat it (Re Lipinski)
On dissolution, surplus to members at that time (Re Bucks Constabulary)
questions.modelAnswer: The club has no legal personality. If its purposes are charitable, such as educational chess open to the public, the gift is a valid charitable trust. Otherwise a purpose trust fails the beneficiary principle (Re Astor [1952]), unless Re Denley [1969] applies. The better view is that the gift goes to the members as an accretion to the funds, held under the club rules (Re Recher [1972]). Under Re Lipinski [1976], "for the purposes of the club" does not defeat this if members can change the rules and divide the assets. If the club is dissolved, any surplus goes to the members at that time (Re Bucks Constabulary Fund (No 2) [1979]).

questions.q: "The fusion of law and equity is a fallacy: the Judicature Acts fused the courts, not the rules." Discuss.
markScheme: Historical background: Chancery, Earl of Oxford's Case, the Judicature Acts 1873–75 and s49 SCA 1981
Ashburner's 'two streams' metaphor: one channel, waters not mingling
Lord Diplock in United Scientific Holdings: fusion of rules
Examples suggesting substantive fusion or cross-fertilisation: equitable compensation for breach of duty of care, Walsh v Lonsdale, set-off, discretionary approaches
Examples showing separate rules: legal vs equitable title and the bona fide purchaser; equitable remedies discretionary; separate tracing rules (common law vs equity); limitation differences
Debate on whether fusion is desirable: coherence vs loss of equity's conscience-based flexibility
Academic positions (eg Burrows for integration; Martin/others cautious)
Modern case law: AIB v Mark Redler aligning compensation with common law principles; Patel v Mirza applying a single illegality approach; Foskett on tracing
Evaluation of the 'fallacy' language
Structured conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The Judicature Acts 1873–75 created one Supreme Court in which every judge could apply both common law and equity. They kept the rule that equity prevails where the two conflict, now in the Senior Courts Act 1981 s49. Ashburner famously said the two streams of jurisdiction ran in the same channel without mingling their waters. On that orthodox view, fusion of the substantive rules is indeed a fallacy.

The evidence for continuing separation is strong. Legal and equitable titles remain distinct, and the bona fide purchaser defence applies only to equitable interests. Equitable remedies are discretionary, while common law damages are available as of right. Tracing still has separate common law and equitable rules, although Foskett v McKeown [2001] hinted at harmonising them. Limitation periods and defences also differ.

There is, however, real cross-fertilisation. Lord Diplock in United Scientific Holdings v Burnley BC [1978] said the systems had become fused, and some later developments support him. Equitable compensation for a trustee's negligence borrows common law ideas of causation and remoteness. AIB Group v Mark Redler [2014] aligned compensation for breach of trust more closely with common law principles. Patel v Mirza [2016] adopted one approach to illegality across contract, unjust enrichment and trusts. Walsh v Lonsdale shows equity changing the practical effect of a legal transaction.

So the statement is accurate about the legislation but too absolute about what followed. The Acts did not fuse the rules, but working in one court has encouraged the doctrines to borrow from each other. Writers favouring integration, such as Andrew Burrows, argue that the remaining divisions are historical accidents that should be removed in the interests of coherence. Others warn that equity's focus on conscience and its flexible remedies would be lost by assimilation. The fiduciary profit rule, which Rukhadze v Recovery Partners [2025] UKSC 10 recently refused to soften, illustrates the distinctive deterrent role that equity can play.

The best view is that we have one legal system containing distinct but interacting bodies of doctrine. Calling fusion a fallacy captures the formal position, but it misses how the two have grown together in substance.

questions.q: Celia's will leaves her residuary estate to Dan "in the hope that he will look after my nieces as he sees fit". She also leaves "most of my wine collection" to trustees for her godson. By a lifetime declaration, she transferred £200,000 to trustees to distribute "among such of my friends and anyone who has ever lived in Manchester as the trustees select". Finally, Celia orally told her trustee Ed to hold her beneficial interest under her father's trust for her sister, and he agreed. Advise on the validity of each disposition.
markScheme: Residuary gift: precatory words, no certainty of intention (Re Adams and the Kensington Vestry; contrast Comiskey); Dan takes absolutely
Whole-document construction and possibility of moral obligation only
Wine: 'most of' is uncertain subject matter (Palmer v Simmonds); tangible goods require identification (Re London Wine; Re Goldcorp)
Failure leads to resulting trust or falls into residue
£200,000: discretionary trust; McPhail is-or-is-not test
'Friends': conceptual uncertainty in a discretionary trust (Re Barlow distinguished, as it concerned individual gifts); Re Baden differing views
'Anyone who has ever lived in Manchester': administrative unworkability (ex p West Yorkshire MCC)
Effect: trust void, resulting trust for Celia
Oral direction: disposition of subsisting equitable interest needs signed writing under s53(1)(c) (Grey v IRC)
Ineffective, so the interest stays with Celia's estate
questions.modelAnswer:
Residuary gift to Dan. The words "in the hope that" are precatory. Since Re Adams and the Kensington Vestry (1884), such words do not usually create a trust unless the whole document shows an intention to impose a binding obligation, as in Comiskey v Bowring-Hanbury [1905]. There is no certainty of intention, so Dan takes the residue absolutely, subject at most to a moral obligation.

Wine. "Most of my wine collection" lacks certainty of subject matter, like "the bulk" in Palmer v Simmonds (1854). Bottles of wine are tangible, so Hunter v Moss [1994], which concerned identical shares, will not help. Re London Wine [1986] and Re Goldcorp [1995] require specific goods to be identified. The gift fails, and the wine falls into residue, which goes to Dan.

The £200,000. This is a discretionary trust, so McPhail v Doulton [1971] applies: can it be said of any given person whether they are or are not within the class? "Friends" is arguably conceptually uncertain. Re Barlow [1979] upheld a gift to friends only because it was a series of individual gifts, a reasoning that does not apply to a discretionary trust. More decisively, "anyone who has ever lived in Manchester" covers millions of people with no meaningful link to Celia. That is likely to be administratively unworkable or capricious under R v District Auditor, ex p West Yorkshire MCC [1986]. The trust fails, and the trustees hold the £200,000 on resulting trust for Celia.

Oral direction to Ed. Celia was directing her trustee to hold her existing equitable interest for her sister. That is a disposition of a subsisting equitable interest, which LPA 1925 s53(1)(c) requires to be in signed writing. Grey v IRC [1960] is directly in point. Vandervell v IRC [1967] does not apply, because no legal title moved. Ed's agreement does not change this. Unless the sister can show a specifically enforceable contract giving rise to a constructive trust under s53(2) (Neville v Wilson [1997]), which is unlikely without consideration, the interest stays with Celia and passes under her will.

questions.q: Fiona's will leaves £100,000 to Gus "on trusts I have communicated to him". The day before signing the will, Fiona told Gus that the money was for her secret son, Hal; Gus nodded. Fiona also left her cottage to Iris absolutely; a week before her death Fiona handed Iris a sealed envelope marked "not to be opened until my death", which contained instructions to hold the cottage for Fiona's carer, Jo. Iris opened it after the funeral. Advise Hal and Jo.
markScheme: Half-secret trust: will refers to a trust; communication before or at execution and consistent with the will (Blackwell; Re Keen)
Communication the day before execution and acceptance by nodding (silence/acquiescence suffices)
Hal's claim succeeds; Gus holds on trust
Fully secret trust: Iris takes absolutely on the face of the will
Communication must be of the fact of the trust and its terms during the testator's life; a sealed envelope counts as constructive communication (Re Keen)
But acceptance: Iris did not know the contents before death; she had the opportunity to refuse? Consider Re Boyes/Ottaway
Standard of proof: ordinary civil standard (Re Snowden)
Justification: dehors the will theory/fraud prevention
Conclusion for each claimant
questions.modelAnswer:
Hal. The will gives £100,000 to Gus "on trusts I have communicated to him". The will shows that a trust exists but not its terms, so this is a half-secret trust. Blackwell v Blackwell [1929] and Re Keen [1937] require the terms to be communicated before or at the time the will is executed, consistently with the will. Fiona told Gus the day before she signed. Communicating before execution is consistent with the will's reference to trusts "communicated", even though the past tense was used. Gus's nod is enough to show acceptance, because silent acquiescence suffices. Hal must prove the trust to the ordinary civil standard (Re Snowden [1979]). He can do that through Gus's evidence. Gus therefore holds the £100,000 on trust for Hal, and if the trust failed Gus could not keep the money himself.

Jo. The cottage is left to Iris absolutely, so any trust would be fully secret. Such a trust needs intention, communication of the trust and its terms during Fiona's lifetime, and acceptance by Iris (Ottaway v Norman [1972]). In Re Keen, the Court of Appeal said that handing over a sealed envelope containing the terms, which the legatee knows contains instructions, is like a ship sailing under sealed orders. It counts as communication, provided the legatee knows she is receiving instructions for a trust. Iris received the envelope during Fiona's lifetime, and its label showed that it contained something important connected with Fiona's death. Whether Iris accepted is less clear. If she understood that it contained directions about the property and took it without objecting, she can be taken to have accepted. If she had no reason to think it concerned a trust, Jo's claim fails and Iris takes the cottage beneficially.

On balance, Hal has a strong claim. Jo's claim depends on what Iris understood the envelope to be when Fiona gave it to her. Evidence of the conversation at the handover will be decisive.

questions.q: Kemal owns shares in a private company whose articles require directors' approval of transfers. Wanting to give 1,000 shares to his niece Lina, he signs a stock transfer form, tells her "the shares are yours", but keeps the form in his desk. He also tells his partner Mia that his car "is yours now" but keeps the keys and continues driving it. On his deathbed in hospital, Kemal gives his friend Nico the key to a box containing deeds to his flat, saying "this is yours if I don't pull through". Kemal dies, appointing Mia as his executor. Advise Lina, Mia and Nico.
markScheme: Milroy v Lord: equity will not perfect an imperfect gift; no declaration of trust implied
Re Rose: donor must do everything in his power; keeping the form means he had not done so
Pennington v Waine: unconscionability; telling Lina and possibly her reliance; criticisms; Zeital and Curtis v Pulbrook
Lina's claim is weak unless Pennington is followed
Car: gift of chattel requires delivery or deed; no delivery while Kemal keeps keys and use
Strong v Bird: Mia appointed executor; continuing intention until death perfects the gift (Re Gonin)
Flat: DMC elements per King v Dubrey: contemplation of death for a specific reason, conditional, and dominion by handing over the means of control
Sen v Headley: land can be the subject of a DMC; delivery of a key to a box containing the deeds suffices
Effect: Kemal's estate (Mia as executor) holds on trust for Nico
Conclusions
questions.modelAnswer:
Lina. Milroy v Lord (1862) shows equity will not perfect an incomplete gift or treat it as a declaration of trust. Under Re Rose [1952], a gift of shares is complete in equity only once the donor has done everything he alone can do, and handing over the signed transfer form is part of that. Kemal kept the form in his desk, so he had not done everything in his power. Lina's best argument is Pennington v Waine [2002], where it was held unconscionable for the donor to recall a gift after assuring the donee and after a further step, the donee's appointment as a director. Lina would need some comparable reliance. Pennington has been heavily criticised and was distinguished in Zeital v Kaye [2010] and Curtis v Pulbrook [2011]. Without reliance, Lina's claim probably fails.

Mia: the car. A gift of a chattel needs delivery or a deed. Kemal kept the keys and carried on driving, so there was no delivery. But Mia is his executor. Under Strong v Bird (1874), an incomplete gift is perfected when the donee becomes the donor's executor, provided the donor's intention to give continued until death (Re Gonin [1979]). Nothing suggests Kemal changed his mind, so Mia takes the car. If the gift is perfected, she does not have to account for it as part of the estate.

Nico: the flat. A donatio mortis causa requires the gift to be made in contemplation of death in the near future for a specific reason, conditional on death, and with dominion over the property handed over (King v Dubrey [2015]). Kemal was in hospital on his deathbed, and the words "if I don't pull through" show the gift was conditional on death. Sen v Headley [1991] held that land can pass by donatio mortis causa where the donor hands over the means of controlling the title deeds, for example the key to a box containing them. Nico's claim therefore probably succeeds, although Sen concerned unregistered land, and it is less clear whether handing over deeds gives dominion over registered land, where title depends on the register. Mia, as executor, holds the flat on trust for Nico and must transfer it to him.

questions.q: Ola's will leaves: (a) £500,000 to trustees "for such charitable or benevolent purposes as they select"; (b) £200,000 "to provide a free coding school for children in Northtown"; (c) £50,000 to maintain her horse Pegasus for life; (d) £100,000 to "the Northtown Disability Trust", which closed in 2020 when its work ended, two years before Ola made her will. Advise the executors.
markScheme: (a) 'charitable or benevolent': not exclusively charitable, void for uncertainty (Chichester Diocesan Fund v Simpson)
Charities Act 2011 s1, exclusivity requirement; no saving under Charitable Trusts (Validation) Act 1954 for a post-1954 will
Resulting trust/residue
(b) Advancement of education (s3(1)(b)); public benefit: children of a town are a sufficient section of the public; free to users

(c) Non-charitable purpose trust; anomalous exception for specific animals (Re Dean); limited to perpetuity period: 'for life' of a horse is not a valid measuring life, and Re Haines/Re Kelly issues; consider 21-year limit
Possible saving via construction: limit to 21 years; otherwise void
(d) Initial failure: the charity ceased before the will took effect
Cy-près needs general charitable intention (Re Rymer; Re Harwood; Re Finger's WT) under s62
Specific named charity ceased existing tends to indicate no general intention; contrast where it continues in another form
Conclusions
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Charitable status requires purposes that are exclusively charitable (Charities Act 2011 s1). "Charitable or benevolent" allows the trustees to choose benevolent purposes that are not charitable. In Chichester Diocesan Fund v Simpson [1944] the same disjunctive wording was fatal. As a private trust, the gift fails for uncertainty, because there is no workable test for "benevolent purposes", and it also fails the beneficiary principle. The £500,000 falls into residue or passes on intestacy.

(b) A free coding school for children advances education under s3(1)(b). The benefit is clear. Children in a whole town are a sufficient section of the public, with no personal nexus, and the school is free, so the poor are not excluded. The gift is charitable and valid.

(c) A trust to maintain a particular animal is one of the anomalous exceptions to the beneficiary principle (Re Dean (1889); Pettingall v Pettingall (1842)). It must not last longer than the common law perpetuity period. Only human lives can be measuring lives, so a trust for the life of a horse does not on its face comply. In Re Haines (1952) the court took judicial notice that a cat would not outlive 21 years, but a horse can live longer than that. Unless the will can be read as limited to 21 years, the gift fails.

(d) The Northtown Disability Trust closed before Ola made her will, so this is initial failure. Cy-près under s62 applies on initial failure only if Ola had a general charitable intention (Re Rymer [1895]). Leaving money to a specific, named institution suggests that Ola meant to benefit that particular body. Where the body has ceased to exist altogether, the courts are slow to find a general intention (Re Harwood [1936]), although they may infer one from the will as a whole, for example from other charitable gifts such as (b). If no general intention is found, the £100,000 lapses. If its work had continued in another body, the gift might take effect in favour of that body.

questions.q: "The public benefit requirement in charity law is applied inconsistently: it is strict for education and religion, generous for poverty, and lacking principle overall." Critically evaluate.
markScheme: Statutory framework: Charities Act 2011 s4, removal of presumption, Charity Commission guidance
Two aspects of public benefit: benefit and public
Personal nexus rule (Oppenheim; Re Compton) and Lord MacDermott's dissent in Oppenheim (questions of degree)
Poverty exception (Dingle v Turner; AG v Charity Commission [2012]): historical and policy explanations
Religion: Gilmour v Coats (unprovable benefit); Re Hetherington (public masses); Neville Estates v Madden (public benefit through congregants mixing in the community)
Education: Re Pinion (worthless collection); ISC case on fee-paying schools
Different heads may justify different tests (Dingle: Lord Cross)
Political purposes and McGovern as related public benefit concern
Evaluation of coherence and possible reforms
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Under Charities Act 2011 s4, every charitable purpose must be for the public benefit, and s4(2) removes any presumption that a purpose under a particular head is beneficial. Public benefit has two aspects. There must be a real benefit, and it must reach the public or a sufficient section of it.

The "public" aspect varies most between the heads. For education, the personal nexus test excludes classes defined by a link to an employer or family (Oppenheim v Tobacco Securities Trust [1951]; Re Compton [1945]). Lord MacDermott dissented in Oppenheim, arguing that the question is one of degree, and a class of over 110,000 employees is hard to call private. In Dingle v Turner [1972], Lord Cross supported treating the issue as a matter of degree and fiscal policy. Poverty trusts, however, may benefit employees or relatives, a rule confirmed by the Upper Tribunal in AG v Charity Commission [2012]. The exception is historical rather than principled.

The "benefit" aspect also varies. For religion, Gilmour v Coats [1949] rejected cloistered prayer because its benefit could not be proved, yet Neville Estates v Madden [1962] accepted that members who attend a place of worship and mix with the community provide a benefit.
