For education, Re Pinion [1965] denied charity to a collection the court considered worthless, which shows judges evaluating merit. The Independent Schools Council case [2011] required fee-charging schools to provide more than token benefit for the poor, but left the trustees to decide how much.

There is a defence. Lord Cross said in Dingle that public benefit depends on the particular head, since different purposes reach the public in different ways. Variation may therefore be reasoned rather than random. The tax privileges that come with charitable status also justify scrutiny of private class trusts.

The statement is partly correct. The variation is real and largely historical, especially the poverty exception. But a context-sensitive approach can be defended. Reform would be best directed at basing the personal nexus test on a clearer rationale, such as preventing tax-subsidised private benefit, applied consistently across all heads.

questions.q: Pia and Quentin lived together unmarried. In 2012 Pia bought a flat in her sole name for £300,000, with a £60,000 deposit from her savings and a mortgage in her name. Quentin had told Pia he couldn't go on the title "because of my bad credit"; Pia replied, "Don't worry, it's ours". Quentin paid for a new kitchen (£15,000) and split the household bills, while Pia paid the mortgage. They separated in 2025, when the flat was worth £500,000. Quentin claims half. Advise him.
markScheme: Sole legal owner: Quentin must establish a common intention constructive trust (Rosset; Stack/Abbott)
Express agreement: 'it's ours' plus excuse for not being on title, analogous to Eves v Eves / Grant v Edwards
Detrimental reliance: kitchen payment and bills; must be referable to the agreement or conduct one would not otherwise undertake
Rosset dicta on contributions; modern view (Abbott; Geary v Rankine) on inference from whole course of dealing
Quantification: whole course of dealing, Stack factors; imputation permissible at quantification stage in sole name cases (Jones v Kernott; Geary v Rankine)
No presumption of equality in a sole name case
Relevant factors: deposit and mortgage from Pia; Quentin's contributions modest; 'ours' suggests sharing
Possible alternative: proprietary estoppel
Likely outcome: a share less than half
TOLATA s14 for declaration and order
questions.modelAnswer:
Pia is the sole legal owner, so Quentin must show a beneficial interest under a common intention constructive trust. He made no direct contribution, so a resulting trust is unavailable.

Acquisition. In Lloyds Bank v Rosset [1991] the House of Lords said the strongest route is an express agreement, arrangement or understanding to share, followed by detrimental reliance. Pia's reply, "don't worry, it's ours", given in response to Quentin's explanation for not being on the title, resembles the excuse cases. In Eves v Eves [1975] and Grant v Edwards [1986], an excuse for not putting the claimant on the title was treated as evidence of an agreement to share. Quentin has a good argument that there was an express common intention that he would have a beneficial interest.

Detrimental reliance. Quentin must show he acted to his detriment in reliance on the understanding. Paying £15,000 for a new kitchen is significant, and is the kind of spending he would not ordinarily make on someone else's property. Splitting bills is weaker evidence. Taken together, though, his conduct probably satisfies the requirement, particularly as Stack v Dowden [2007] and Abbott v Abbott [2007] encourage a broader look at the parties' whole course of dealing.

Quantification. In a sole-name case there is no starting presumption of equal shares. Jones v Kernott [2011] and Geary v Rankine [2012] allow the court, once a common intention to share has been shown, to infer or if necessary impute shares that are fair in light of the whole course of dealing. Pia provided the deposit and paid the mortgage, so the main financial contributions came from her. Quentin's kitchen and share of the bills, together with the words "it's ours", support a real share but not necessarily half. The likely result is a share well below half, but the exact figure depends on the evidence.

As an alternative, Quentin could plead proprietary estoppel, based on Pia's assurance and his reliance on it. He should apply under TOLATA s14 for a declaration of his share and an order for sale or a buy-out.

questions.q: "After Stack v Dowden and Jones v Kernott, the law on the family home is a judicial creation that pays lip service to intention while delivering whatever the court thinks fair." Discuss.
markScheme: Background: lack of statutory regime for cohabitants; Law Commission 2007 report (Cohabitation) not implemented
Rosset's narrow approach and criticism
Stack: joint names presumption; list of factors; holistic approach; Baroness Hale's emphasis on context
Jones v Kernott: inference vs imputation; imputation permitted at quantification only
Critique: intention fiction, uncertainty, cost of litigation; Lord Neuberger's dissent in Stack favouring resulting trust
Defence: imputation is limited; parties' actual intentions are the primary inquiry; fairness is evaluated by reference to the whole course of dealing
Geary v Rankine and Marr v Collie: limits on context and extension to investment
Comparison with proprietary estoppel's remedial discretion
Reform options: statutory scheme (Law Commission), Scottish model, Family Law (Cohabitation) proposals
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
England has no statutory property regime for cohabitants. The Law Commission's 2007 proposals for a cohabitation scheme were not enacted, so disputes are decided under trust law. The old approach in Lloyds Bank v Rosset [1991] was narrow. It required an express agreement or direct contributions to the price, which disadvantaged partners who contributed in other ways.

Stack v Dowden [2007] changed direction. Where a home is in joint names, the starting point is a beneficial joint tenancy. A party who says otherwise must show a different common intention, judged from the whole course of dealing, with a list of relevant factors. Jones v Kernott [2011] distinguished inference, meaning finding what the parties actually intended from their conduct, from imputation, meaning attributing to them an intention they never had. Imputation is allowed only to quantify shares, and only where it is clear the parties intended to share but no intention about the size of the shares can be found. Then the court awards what is fair having regard to the whole course of dealing.

The statement's criticism has force. Intention found from a wide range of conduct is close to a fiction. Lord Neuberger, dissenting in Stack, preferred the more predictable resulting trust approach. The open list of factors makes outcomes unpredictable and litigation costly, and arguably gives judges a disguised redistributive power.

There is also a defence. Imputation is narrowly confined. In a sole-name case the claimant must still prove an actual common intention to share before any imputation, as Geary v Rankine [2012] shows. Fairness in Kernott is fairness measured against what the parties did, not a free-standing jurisdiction. Marr v Collie [2017] shows that context is still examined closely.

On balance, the statement is exaggerated but contains a real truth. The doctrine is judge-made and does involve evaluative judgment, but within limits based on the parties' conduct. The deeper problem is the lack of legislation. A statutory scheme based on financial contributions and losses, as the Law Commission proposed, would be more honest and predictable than stretching the language of intention.

questions.q: Rhys and Sian are trustees of a £2m family trust. Without taking advice, they invest 80% of the fund in shares of Tidal Ltd, a start-up run by Rhys's nephew, because they "believe in green energy". They never review the investment. Tidal fails and the shares become worthless. The remaining 20% was held in cash for ten years. The beneficiaries sue. Advise the trustees.
markScheme: General power of investment (TA 2000 s3)
Standard investment criteria: suitability and diversification (s4); 80% concentration in a single start-up fails both
Duty to review (s4(2)) breached
Duty to take advice (s5) breached
Duty of care (s1) applies to the investment functions
Ethical motives: Cowan v Scargill (financial interests paramount); possible conflict of interest because of the nephew
Cash holding: failure to invest the remaining 20% (Nestle; loss must be proved)
Measure of compensation: restore the fund; causation (Target; AIB); comparison with what a prudent portfolio would have achieved
Defences: s61 unlikely (unreasonable); exemption clause (Armitage) if any; limitation (six years, s21(3)) for the cash claim may limit recovery
Joint and several liability; contribution between Rhys and Sian
questions.modelAnswer:
Rhys and Sian had power to invest under TA 2000 s3, subject to the statutory duties and the s1 duty of care.

Standard investment criteria. Section 4 required them to consider whether the investment was suitable and whether the fund needed to be diversified. Putting 80% of a £2m family fund into one unproven start-up fails both tests. A speculative single holding is unsuitable for a family trust, and concentrating the fund this way is the opposite of diversification. They also never reviewed the investment, in breach of s4(2).

Advice. Section 5 required them to obtain and consider proper advice unless they reasonably concluded it was unnecessary. For an investment of £1.6m, advice was plainly necessary.

Motive and conflict. Cowan v Scargill [1985] holds that trustees must put the beneficiaries' financial interests first. Their belief in green energy is no justification unless the investment was also financially sound, and Butler-Sloss [2022] concerned charities whose purposes conflicted with certain investments. The family connection with Rhys's nephew also raises a possible conflict of interest, which makes their decision harder to defend.

Cash. Holding 20% in cash for ten years probably also breached the duty to invest for both income and capital growth. Under Nestle v NatWest [1993], however, the beneficiaries must prove that a properly managed fund would have performed better.

Compensation. The trustees must restore the fund to the position it would have been in without the breach. Under Target Holdings [1996] and AIB v Mark Redler [2014], causation is assessed with hindsight, and the comparison is with a prudent, diversified portfolio. Rhys and Sian are jointly and severally liable, and may seek contribution from each other under the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978.

Defences. Section 61 relief requires the trustees to have acted reasonably, which they did not. An exemption clause in the trust instrument could protect them against negligence, but not dishonesty (Armitage v Nurse [1998]). Under the Limitation Act 1980 s21(3), claims about losses more than six years old may be time-barred, which could limit recovery for the cash holding. Liability for the Tidal losses appears clear.

questions.q: Tara is a trustee of the Uplands Trust, which owns 30% of Vale Ltd. Through attending Vale board meetings as the trust's nominee, Tara learns that Vale's neighbouring land is about to be rezoned. The trust deed forbids the trustees from buying land. Tara buys the land personally, sells it a year later for a £400,000 profit, and uses £100,000 to buy a painting now worth £250,000. She also accepted a £20,000 "introduction fee" from a broker to whom she directed trust business. Advise the beneficiaries.
markScheme: Tara is a fiduciary (trustee); the no-conflict and no-profit rules
Opportunity/information obtained by reason of her position (Boardman v Phipps; Regal)
Trust's inability to buy is irrelevant (Regal; Keech v Sandford); Rukhadze reaffirms strictness
No fully informed consent of the beneficiaries
Remedy: profits held on constructive trust (Boardman; FHR); account of profits
Proprietary claim allows tracing into the painting and capture of its increase (Foskett; Reid)
Equitable allowance for skill and work (Boardman; Guinness v Saunders limits); unlikely to be generous where conflict was obvious
Introduction fee: a secret commission/bribe, held on constructive trust (FHR)
Breach of duty also justifies removal of the trustee
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
As a trustee, Tara owes fiduciary duties not to place herself in a position where her interests conflict with her duty and not to profit from her position without fully informed consent (Bray v Ford [1896]).

The land profit. Tara learned of the rezoning while attending Vale board meetings as the trust's nominee. The information and the opportunity came to her because of her fiduciary position, as in Boardman v Phipps [1967]. It is irrelevant that the trust deed prevented the trust from buying land. In Regal (Hastings) v Gulliver [1942] the company's inability to take the opportunity was no defence, and in Keech v Sandford (1726) the trustee was liable although the landlord would not renew to the trust. In Rukhadze v Recovery Partners [2025] UKSC 10 the Supreme Court refused to soften the rule by asking whether the fiduciary would have made the profit anyway. Without fully informed consent from all the beneficiaries, Tara must account for the £400,000.

Proprietary remedy. Following Boardman and FHR European Ventures v Cedar Capital [2014], the profit is held on constructive trust. That allows the beneficiaries to trace. £100,000 of the profit was used to buy the painting, so they can claim the painting itself, now worth £250,000, including its increase in value (Foskett v McKeown [2001]; AG for Hong Kong v Reid [1994]). They can claim the remaining £300,000, or what it represents, either by tracing or through a personal account.

Allowance. Boardman granted an equitable allowance for the fiduciaries' skill and work. Guinness v Saunders [1990] shows the courts give allowances sparingly, especially where the conflict was obvious. Tara acted secretly, so any allowance is likely to be small or refused.

The introduction fee. A payment from a third party to a fiduciary for directing business is a secret commission. Under FHR it is held on constructive trust for the beneficiaries, and the broker may also be liable for dishonest assistance if it knew the circumstances.

The beneficiaries should claim the painting and an account of the remaining profits, recover the £20,000, and seek Tara's removal as trustee.

questions.q: Will, a trustee, takes £50,000 from the Xavier Trust and £30,000 from the Yates Trust and pays both into his personal account, which held £20,000 of his own money. He withdraws £40,000 to buy shares now worth £80,000, and then spends £50,000 on a cruise. He then pays in £10,000 of his own money. The account now holds £20,000. Will is bankrupt. Advise both trusts on their proprietary claims. (Assume the trust payments were made before any withdrawal.)
markScheme: Tracing as a process; equitable tracing available as there is a fiduciary relationship (Foskett)
Balance after deposits: £100,000 (£20k own, £50k X, £30k Y)
Re Hallett: trustee presumed to spend own money first, but Re Oatway lets beneficiaries claim the shares bought
Beneficiaries vs trustee: trusts can elect to claim the shares (worth £80,000) as against Will's own money
Between the two innocent trusts: proportionate sharing (Barlow Clowes; Russell-Cooke) rather than Clayton's Case
Calculation: X 5/8 and Y 3/8 of trust money (£80,000 total)
Lowest intermediate balance: after withdrawals the balance fell to £10,000; later £10,000 of own money is not trust money (Roscoe v Winder)
Allocation: claims over shares (£80,000) and £10,000 of the balance shared 5:3
Show the figures: shares X £50,000 / Y £30,000; balance X £6,250 / Y £3,750
Bankruptcy: proprietary claims take priority over unsecured creditors; residual personal claims
questions.modelAnswer:
The trusts can trace in equity because Will owed them fiduciary duties (Foskett v McKeown [2001]). After the deposits, the account held £100,000: £20,000 of Will's own money, £50,000 from Xavier and £30,000 from Yates.

Withdrawals. Will first spent £40,000 on shares, then £50,000 on a cruise, leaving £10,000. Between a trustee and the beneficiaries, Re Hallett (1880) presumes that the trustee spends his own money first. Re Oatway [1903] lets the beneficiaries claim an asset bought from the mixed fund where the remaining money has later been spent. The trusts will therefore attribute the shares, now worth £80,000, to trust money. On that analysis the cruise used Will's £20,000 and £30,000 of trust money, which cannot be traced.

Lowest intermediate balance. After the withdrawals the balance was £10,000. Will's later deposit of £10,000 is not treated as repaying the trusts unless he intended it to (Roscoe v Winder [1915]). The trusts can therefore claim £10,000 of the current £20,000 balance, and the rest belongs to Will's estate.

Between the two trusts. Both are innocent, so the courts usually reject Clayton's Case (first in, first out) in favour of sharing in proportion to contributions (Barlow Clowes v Vaughan [1992]; Russell-Cooke v Prentis [2002]). The trusts contributed £80,000 in the ratio 5:3.
- Shares worth £80,000: Xavier £50,000 and Yates £30,000.
- Account balance of £10,000: Xavier £6,250 and Yates £3,750.

Both assets are traceable proceeds of trust money, so the trusts can claim both. Xavier recovers £56,250 and Yates £33,750. The amount above what they contributed reflects the gain on the shares, which belongs to them (Foskett). If the shares had fallen in value, the trusts could instead have taken a lien over them for the £40,000 spent.

Proprietary claims take priority over Will's unsecured creditors in his bankruptcy. Here the trusts recover more than they lost, so they need no personal claim against Will.

questions.q: Zed, a trustee of a pension trust, dishonestly transferred £2m of trust money to Aero Ltd as part of a scheme to defraud the beneficiaries. Aero's managing director, Bea, a chartered accountant, set up the payment structure; she suspected the money was not Zed's but deliberately asked no questions because the fee was attractive. Aero received the money into its own account and then paid £1m to Coral Bank to discharge Aero's overdraft and £1m to Dina, Zed's partner, as a gift; Dina believed Zed had won it gambling. Advise the beneficiaries on their claims against Bea, Aero, Coral Bank and Dina.
markScheme: Breach of trust by Zed (dishonest); personal liability to restore
Dishonest assistance against Bea: breach, assistance, dishonesty (Royal Brunei v Tan)
Dishonesty test: Barlow Clowes, Ivey, Group Seven; blind-eye knowledge suffices
Bea's liability is personal, joint and several with Zed; six-year limitation (Williams v Central Bank of Nigeria)
Knowing receipt against Aero: beneficial receipt of trust property in breach; knowledge attributed via its directing mind (Bea) makes retention unconscionable (Akindele)

Coral Bank: receipt in discharge of a debt; a bank receiving in reduction of an overdraft is a beneficial recipient, but likely a bona fide purchaser for value without notice; tracing into a paid-off overdraft is generally impossible (Bishopsgate v Homan), subject to backwards tracing (Brazil v Durant)
Dina: volunteer recipient; proprietary claim to traceable money in her hands; no knowing receipt liability without unconscionable knowledge
Change of position defence against personal unjust enrichment claims; not against proprietary claim where asset retained
Byers v Saudi National Bank: requires continuing equitable interest at receipt (present here)
Prioritisation of claims and remedies; conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Zed is personally liable for the £2m, but the third parties matter more.

Bea: dishonest assistance. Zed committed a breach of trust, and Bea helped him by setting up the payment structure. Under Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan [1995] she is liable if she acted dishonestly. Dishonesty is judged objectively, by the standards of ordinary decent people, against what Bea actually knew or suspected (Barlow Clowes v Eurotrust [2005]; Ivey v Genting [2017]; Group Seven v Notable Services [2019]). She suspected the money was not Zed's and deliberately asked no questions. That deliberate blindness is dishonest, especially for an accountant. She is liable jointly and severally with Zed for the full £2m, subject to the six-year limitation period confirmed in Williams v Central Bank of Nigeria [2014].

Aero: knowing receipt. Aero received the trust money for its own benefit, in breach of trust. Bea was its directing mind, so her knowledge is attributed to Aero, making it unconscionable for Aero to keep the benefit (BCCI v Akindele [2001]). The beneficiaries' equitable interest still existed when Aero received the money, as Byers v Saudi National Bank [2023] requires. Aero is liable to account for £2m.

Coral Bank. When money is used to pay off an overdraft, the debt is extinguished and there is nothing left to trace into (Bishopsgate v Homan [1995]). Backwards tracing under Federal Republic of Brazil v Durant [2015] needs coordination between the overdraft and the misappropriation, and there is no evidence of that. The bank gave value by discharging the debt and had no relevant knowledge, so it is effectively a bona fide purchaser.

Dina. Dina believed the money came from gambling, so she lacks the knowledge needed for liability in knowing receipt.
